title: Buddha (as the tradition tells it)
tomorrow: one name in the ten is still written 'will be.' which one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lunch table: some Hindu texts tell the Buddha as Vishnu's descent, and Buddhists tell him as their own teacher. Then Dawa asked a question back: which ten do you count?

Every family has the recipe, and every aunt's version of the recipe is different. Priya takes Dawa's question to Nani, who counts on her fingers without looking up from the stove: fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, dwarf, Parashurama, Rama, Balarama, Krishna, Kalki. Priya checks the list on her phone. Fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, dwarf, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, Buddha, Kalki. Same ten fingers, a different name on one of them. And Nani, stirring, isn't bothered at all. Why not?
screen: `EVERY AUNT'S RECIPE DIFFERS.` → `NANI'S TEN. THE PHONE'S TEN.` → `WHY ISN'T NANI BOTHERED?`

segments.voice: Start with the Bhagavata. Its first list doesn't stop at ten. It names Balarama and Krishna side by side, then the Buddha, then Kalki still to come, with sages and kings along the way. Then it says the descents are beyond counting, like streams running without end from a lake that never empties. Now Jayadeva's hymn. It does sing ten forms, and among them are Balarama with his plow, then the Buddha, then Kalki. Krishna isn't in his ten at all. That's because the whole hymn is sung to Krishna, as Keshava, the one who takes every form. So one poet keeps both Balarama and the Buddha and lifts Krishna out of the line to stand behind it. Other lists, like Nani's, keep Krishna in the line and give the other place to Balarama. Here's the puzzle, solved. Ten is a frame, not a fence. The tradition keeps the frame and lets more than one set of names stand inside it, and the Bhagavata itself says the lake was never going to fit on ten fingers. Priya texts Dawa a photo of both lists. Dawa writes back: so nobody's list is wrong? Priya types: nobody's list is the whole lake.
screen: `THE BHAGAVATA: MORE THAN TEN.` · `STREAMS FROM A LAKE THAT NEVER EMPTIES.` · `JAYADEVA: KRISHNA BEHIND THE LINE.` · `NANI'S TEN: BALARAMA AND KRISHNA.` · then, large: `TEN IS A FRAME, NOT A FENCE.`

segments.voice: Count ten slowly on your fingers, any list you like, one breath for each finger, and let your hands fall open at ten. Then keep sitting with your hands open, and let the breath run on past the count, like a stream that doesn't stop.
Buddha: counted among the ten in some Hindu lists and left out of others, where Balarama stands in his place.
Your line: Buddha, as the tradition tells it. The lake doesn't run dry, and the list doesn't hold still. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: Dawa asks: if Krishna isn't in Jayadeva's ten, did Jayadeva leave him out on purpose?
options: not to drop him: the whole hymn is sung to Krishna, the one who takes every form.
yes: Jayadeva honored Balarama and the Buddha more than Krishna.
yes: Krishna's stories weren't known yet when Jayadeva wrote.
fork.reveal: Jayadeva's refrain addresses Keshava, Krishna, in every verse; Krishna stands behind the line of ten rather than in it.

original.note: Sanskrit asankhyeya: beyond counting, the Bhagavata's word for the descents.

chat.meaning: The Bhagavata's own list runs past ten and calls the descents beyond counting, and Jayadeva's ten differ again. More than one ten is kept.

Balarama.meaning: Krishna's brother, counted in some lists of ten

Keshava.meaning: a name of Krishna; Jayadeva's hymn is sung to him

Kalki.meaning: the form of Vishnu still to come

Parashurama.meaning: Vishnu's form as a sage's son with an axe
